## Head et al 2015 (PubMed/Medline)

**Reference:**
@head2015extent.

**Research question:**
extent of p-hacking and its impact on meta-analyses.

**Data collection:**
The source comprises open-access PubMed papers published up to 2014. The authors used regular expressions to extract p-values from the text of the Abstract and Results sections, but not from tables. The downloaded data contain about 220,000 studies and about 2 million rows.

**Data availability:**
The dataset is available at <https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.79d43> under a CC0 1.0 Universal licence.

**Data processing:**
We followed the same minimal clean-up steps (e.g. removing values found in large supplementary sections) as the original paper and also attached PubMed IDs to the dataset using DOI lookup.
The article DOIs were supplied in the source data; we obtained the PubMed IDs
through Europe PMC. Both identifiers are retained, with `doi` duplicating
the source's `first.doi` field.

When constructing the BEAR dataset, we derived unsigned z-values from p-values.
We treated p-values recorded as exactly 0 as truncated and set the z-operator
to `>`. We recoded all inequalities to sharp inequalities.
For the distributed version of BEAR 50,000 studies are selected at random, with
one row per study, in order to keep the file size manageable.

**Study characteristics:**

- **Study ID:** we use the PubMed identifier (`pmid`).
- **Topic:** we use the journal-level Field-of-Research classification (`Category`).
- `subset` distinguishes abstract extraction from full text/results extraction.

- The dataset does not have study designs.
- The extracted p-values are converted to z-values.
- We do not know the underlying effect measures.
- `subset` distinguishes abstract extraction from results-text extraction.
